content: 1. Wekesah FM, Kyobutungi C, Grobbee DE, Klipstein-Grobusch K conducted a qualitative study to explore the understanding and perceptions of cardiovascular diseases and their risk factors among residents of urban informal settlements in Nairobi. This study was published in BMJ Open in 2019. 2. Negesa LB, Magarey J, Rasmussen P, and Hendriks JML investigated the knowledge of patients in Ethiopia regarding cardiovascular risk factors and associated lifestyle behaviors through a cross-sectional study conducted in 2018. The findings were published in PLoS One in 2020. 3. Oli N, Vaidya A, Subedi M, and Krettek A conducted in-depth interviews in a peri-urban Nepalese community to understand the experiences and perceptions of individuals with cardiometabolic conditions regarding the causes and prevention of cardiovascular diseases. The results were published in Global Health Action in 2014. 4. Erhardt L and Hobbs FD examined public perceptions of cardiovascular risk across five European countries through the REACT survey. Their findings were published in the International Journal of Clinical Practice in 2002. 5. Manafe M, Chelule PK, and Madiba S explored South African adults' views on their body weight and the perceived risks of developing obesity and non-communicable diseases (NCDs). This study was published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health in 2021. 6. Akindele MO, Phillips JS, and Igumbor EU analyzed the relationship between body fat percentage and body mass index (BMI) in overweight and obese individuals in an urban African setting. Their findings were published in the Journal of Public Health in Africa in 2016. 7. Bosire EN, Cohen E, Erzse A, Goldstein SJ, Hofman KJ, and Norris SA investigated the normalization of obesity in urban-poor South African communities, with participants often stating, I’d say I’m fat, I’m not obese. This study was published in Public Health Nutrition in 2020. 8. Collins AA, Gloria EO, and Matilda S-A studied the preferred body size among urban Ghanaian women and its implications for the overweight and obesity problem. Their findings were published in the Pan African Medical Journal in 2016. 9. Agyapong NAF, Annan RA, Apprey C, and Aduku LNE examined body weight perceptions, obesity awareness, and actions taken to achieve desired weight among rural and urban Ghanaian adults. This study was published in the Journal of Obesity in 2020. 10. Frayon S, Cherrier S, Cavaloc Y, Wattelez G, Touitou A, Zongo P, et al. reported on the misperception of weight status among rural and urban adolescents aged 11 to 16 years in New Caledonia. Their preliminary findings were published in BMC Public Health in 2017. 11. Mattes RD and Popkin BM reviewed the effects of non-nutritive sweetener consumption on appetite and food intake, as well as the potential mechanisms involved. This review was published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2009. 12. The World Health Organization (WHO) published guidelines on sugar intake for adults and children, emphasizing the importance of reducing sugar consumption to improve health outcomes. These guidelines were accessed in January 2023. 13. Data on food prices and spending trends were made available through a government website, providing insights into agricultural and food statistics. This resource was accessed in January 2023. 14. A map illustrating which countries spend the most on food was published on a website, offering a global perspective on food expenditure. This information was accessed in January 2023. 15. A report on poverty trends in South Africa examined absolute poverty levels between 2006 and 2011, providing valuable insights into socioeconomic disparities. This report was accessed in January 2023. 16. Wang YC, Coxson P, Shen YM, Goldman L, and Bibbins-Domingo K analyzed the potential health and economic benefits of implementing a penny-per-ounce tax on sugar-sweetened beverages to reduce the burden of diabetes. Their findings were published in Health Affairs in 2012. 17. Long MW, Gortmaker SL, Ward ZJ, Resch SC, Moodie ML, Sacks G, et al. evaluated the cost-effectiveness of a sugar-sweetened beverage excise tax in the United States. Their study was published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine in 2015. 18. Lal A, Mantilla-Herrera AM, Veerman L, Backholer K, Sacks G, Moodie M, et al. modeled the health benefits of a sugar-sweetened beverage tax across different socioeconomic groups in Australia, analyzing cost-effectiveness and equity. Their findings were published in PLoS Medicine in 2017. 19. Basto-Abreu A, Barrientos-Gutiérrez T, Vidaña-Pérez D, Colchero MA, Hernández FM, Hernández-Ávila M, et al. assessed the cost-effectiveness of the sugar-sweetened beverage excise tax in Mexico. Their study was published in Health Affairs in 2019. 20. Lee Y, Mozaffarian D, Sy S, Liu J, Wilde PE, Marklund M, et al. conducted a microsimulation study to evaluate the health impact and cost-effectiveness of various sugar-sweetened beverage tax policies in the United States. Their findings were published in Circulation in 2020. 21. Lobstein T, Neveux M, and Landon J reviewed the costs, equity, and acceptability of three obesity prevention policies to support policy development. Their narrative review was published in Obesity Science & Practice in 2020. 22. Allen L, Williams J, Townsend N, Mikkelsen B, Roberts N, Foster C, et al. systematically reviewed the relationship between socioeconomic status and behavioral risk factors for non-communicable diseases in lowand lower-middle-income countries. Their findings were published in The Lancet Global Health in 2017. 23. Dinsa GD, Goryakin Y, Fumagalli E, and Suhrcke M systematically reviewed the association between obesity and socioeconomic status in developing countries. Their findings were published in Obesity Reviews in 2012. 24. Vazquez CE and Cubbin C reviewed literature from the past decade to explore the relationship between socioeconomic status and childhood obesity, aiming to inform intervention research. Their review was published in Current Obesity Reports in 2020. 25. Newton S, Braithwaite D, and Akinyemiju TF conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to examine the impact of socioeconomic status over the life course on obesity. Their findings were published in PLoS One in 2017. 26. Caro JC, Corvalán C, Reyes M, Silva A, Popkin B, and Taillie LS evaluated the impact of Chile’s 2014 sugar-sweetened beverage tax on prices and purchases in an urban environment. Their observational study was published in PLoS Medicine in 2018. 27. Nakamura R, Mirelman AJ, Cuadrado C, Silva-Illanes N, Dunstan J, and Suhrcke M assessed the effects of Chile’s 2014 sugar-sweetened beverage tax in urban areas through an observational study. Their findings were published in PLoS Medicine in 2018. 28. Lobstein T, Neveux M, and Landon J reviewed the costs, equity, and acceptability of three obesity prevention policies to support policy development. Their narrative review was published in Obesity Science & Practice in 2020. 29. Frohlich KL and Potvin L discussed the inequality paradox in public health practice, emphasizing the need to address vulnerable populations through a population-based approach. Their article was published in the American Journal of Public Health in 2008. 30. The Global Database on the Implementation of Nutrition Action (GINA) provides comprehensive information on nutrition-related policies and actions worldwide. This resource was accessed in January 2023. 31. The WHO guideline on the use of non-sugar sweeteners offers evidence-based recommendations for their use in dietary practices. This guideline was accessed in January 2023. 32. Food-based dietary guidelines are available on a website, providing practical advice for healthy eating patterns. This resource was accessed in January 2023. 33. Russell C, Baker P, Grimes C, Lindberg R, and Lawrence MA analyzed global trends in the use of added sugars and non-nutritive sweeteners in packaged foods, discussing the implications for public health. Their study was published in Public Health Nutrition in 2022. 34. Sylvetsky AC and Dietz WH examined the potential for nutrient-content claims to either guide or confuse consumers. Their article was published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2014. 35. Sylvetsky AC, Greenberg M, Zhao X, and Rother KI conducted a pilot study to explore parents’ perceptions of giving non-nutritive sweeteners to their children. Their findings were published in the International Journal of Pediatrics in 2014. 36. Williams P reviewed consumer understanding and use of health claims on food products, highlighting the challenges and opportunities in this area. This review was published in Nutrition Reviews in 2005. 37. Hodgkins CE, Egan B, Peacock M, Klepacz N, Miklavec K, Pravst I, et al. developed a consumer-derived typology to understand how consumers categorize health-related claims on food products. Their study was published in Nutrients in 2019. 38. Wills JM, Storcksdieck genannt Bonsmann S, Kolka M, and Grunert KG investigated European consumers’ attitudes, understanding, and purchasing behavior related to health claims on food products. Their findings were published in the Proceedings of the Nutrition Society in 2012. 39. De Boer A reviewed 15 years of regulating nutrition and health claims in Europe, discussing past achievements, current challenges, and future directions. This review was published in Nutrients in 2021. 40. Van der Horst K, Bucher T, Duncanson K, Murawski B, and Labbe D conducted a scoping review to examine consumer understanding, perception, and interpretation of serving size information on food labels. Their findings were published in Nutrients in 2019.
